title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: A cyberattack pushed all three North Carolina Ports facilities into manual gate processing
items.content_text: North Carolina Ports Authority suffered a cyberattack on 4 August that disrupted IT systems and slowed operations at the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port. The systems-wide outage forced a switch to manual gate processing, delaying truckers and cargo moves across all three facilities. The authority detected and contained the incident the same day and reported operations returning to normal by 7 August, with some delays persisting during IT restoration. No evidence of sensitive data compromise has been reported, and no threat actor has been named. Wilmington alone handles roughly 5,000 container gate moves a week. The incident is a reminder that terminal gates, vessel scheduling, documentation and cargo release are now operational systems in their own right.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: North Carolina Ports Authority disclosures — via The Maritime Executive and Splash247

items.title: A breach at Ceva Logistics halted shipments from eight European warehouses and rippled into retail
items.content_text: A cyber intrusion disrupted part of Ceva Logistics’ European contract-logistics operation from 29 July, halting shipments at eight warehouses and delaying deliveries for retail customers holding inventory there. Affected customers were notified on 1 August. Personal data including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and order details was compromised, though Ceva says payment and credential data was not. Dutch retailers Bol and De Bijenkorf, ING, Ace & Tate, football club Ajax and Valve have been reported as affected downstream. The Dutch Data Protection Authority is investigating. No ransomware group has claimed responsibility and Ceva has not disclosed technical details. For terminal and shipping operators, this is the landside failure mode: cargo does not move because the systems that release it are down.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: The Record and SecurityWeek, citing Ceva customer notifications

items.title: Baltic GNSS interference is accelerating — Bornholm has already logged more disruption in 2026 than in all of 2025
items.content_text: A monitoring station on the Danish island of Bornholm has recorded 30 cases of navigation-signal jamming and spoofing so far in 2026, against 16 for all of 2025 and 11 in 2024. Denmark has reported record numbers and durations of GPS disruption in the Baltic; the cargo ship Saturn lost signal for about a day between Gdańsk and southern Gotland on 29 July, and again on a later voyage as far as Bornholm. A Polish study suggests some of the interference originates from vessels rather than fixed shore sites, which would make the source mobile and harder to avoid. Several European governments attribute the activity to Russia. This is electronic warfare rather than a cyber compromise, but the operational consequence — loss of position, timing and AIS integrity — lands on the same bridge team.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Danish and Polish monitoring reporting — via Splash247 and Technology.org

items.title: Gunra ransomware is entering through unpatched VPNs and firewalls, with transport named in its victim base
items.content_text: The FBI, CISA, DoD Cyber Crime Center, NSA, US Secret Service and the Republic of Korea’s National Police Agency issued #StopRansomware advisory AA26-222A on Gunra, a Conti-derived double-extortion operation that moved to a structured affiliate model in early 2026. Transport is explicitly among its named victim sectors, alongside manufacturing, utilities and government. Affiliates gain access through exposed edge infrastructure — VPN gateways, firewall appliances and RDP — including the Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy authentication-bypass flaws CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472. For ports and shipping companies, the relevant exposure is usually the remote-access appliance serving terminal staff, agents and vessel connectivity, which is often maintained on a different cadence from the rest of the estate.

items.title: A suspected China-nexus actor is mass-exploiting a patched vCenter flaw and deploying ransomware
items.content_text: Exploitation of CVE-2026-59310, a directory-traversal flaw in Broadcom VMware vCenter rated CVSS 9.8 and patched on 29 July, has been attributed to a suspected China-nexus actor. German incident-response firm QUIRSO counted roughly 361 victim IP addresses across 47 countries, 343 appearing between 3 and 5 August, and assesses with moderate confidence that a Chinese-speaking operator is responsible. The chain persists through cron, systemd and reverse_ssh, drops a Linux backdoor and in some cases deploys Babuk-derived ransomware. Terminal operating systems, berth planning, gate systems and shore-side vessel-traffic applications are commonly virtualised on a single cluster, so root on vCenter is a plausible route to the same manual-gate scenario North Carolina Ports just lived through.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: The Hacker News, reporting QUIRSO research

items.title: Dragos counted 95 ransomware incidents at transportation and logistics organisations in Q2
items.content_text: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents at industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, a 12 percent rise on Q1, with transportation and logistics groups accounting for 95 and North America for 514 overall. Manufacturing absorbed the bulk at 747. The finding most relevant to maritime is what Dragos did not see: no ransomware operator directly manipulated an industrial control system during the quarter. Disruption came from encrypted enterprise IT and from precautionary shutdowns of virtualisation and shared infrastructure. That matches both the North Carolina Ports and Ceva incidents this month — cargo stopped moving because business systems went down, not because anyone reached a crane PLC.

items.title: Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway carries an unauthenticated root command-injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-02 covers CVE-2026-19188, an operating-system command-injection vulnerability in the Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway rated CVSS 10.0. The Net Check feature reachable through the /setting endpoint passes unsanitised input to the cmdPing Socket.io event, letting an attacker run arbitrary commands as root. CISA lists Critical Manufacturing, Energy and Water and Wastewater among affected sectors; Haiwell has released fixed firmware. Ports and terminals should still check, because low-cost cloud HMI gateways of this type turn up in shoreside building management, fuelling, conveyor and bulk-handling installations, usually fitted by a contractor and rarely recorded in the port’s own asset register. No public exploitation has been reported to CISA.

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: a maximum-severity SIMATIC IoT2050 flaw leads ten Siemens advisories
items.content_text: Siemens, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact published their August ICS Patch Tuesday advisories. Siemens issued ten, the most serious a maximum-severity missing-authentication vulnerability in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker execute code with elevated privileges on the underlying server. Terminals and vessels run more Siemens and Schneider equipment than the maritime conversation usually acknowledges — crane drives, shore power, conveyor lines, bunkering and building systems — and IoT2050-class gateways are a common way of getting that data to a shore-side dashboard. Nothing here is reported as exploited, so this belongs in the planned maintenance queue rather than an emergency change.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: SecurityWeek, summarising Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact advisories

items.title: An actively exploited Cisco ASA and FTD flaw joins the KEV catalogue
items.content_text: CISA added three vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 August: CVE-2026-20349, a heap inspection vulnerability in Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Firepower Threat Defense; CVE-2026-68820 in the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock; and CVE-2026-72898, a SQL injection flaw in Metabase. The Cisco entry matters most for maritime because ASA appliances commonly terminate shore-office VPNs, connect terminals to headquarters and front third-party access for equipment vendors and agents. KEV listing means confirmed exploitation in the wild. Together with the Gunra advisory, the August pattern for this sector is consistent: intrusions start at a known-vulnerable perimeter appliance, not at anything maritime-specific.

items.title: Fifteen ICS advisories in one day, spanning access control, energy and engineering tools
items.content_text: CISA published 15 industrial control system advisories on 13 August, after three on 11 August and two on 4 August. The batch includes Johnson Controls Airwall, Hitachi Energy’s APM Edge product and ANDRITZ HIPASE-250 and 250 SCALA. Earlier August advisories covered Schneider Electric Saitel remote terminal units, Mitsubishi Electric CPU modules and Delta Electronics engineering tools. Ports should read this batch with physical security in mind as much as process control: Johnson Controls products sit behind a great deal of terminal access control and building management, and a separate CISA advisory this cycle covers a critical deserialisation flaw in C•CURE 9000 and victor application servers. None of the items carries reported active exploitation.

items.title: The USCG cyber rule’s full compliance date is July 2027 — incident reporting is already mandatory
items.content_text: The Coast Guard’s final rule on Cybersecurity in the Marine Transportation System, published under MTSA in January 2025, took effect on 16 July 2025 and phases in from there. The cybersecurity training requirement for personnel with access to IT or OT systems fell due on 12 January 2026, and the full compliance date — Cybersecurity Plan, designated Cybersecurity Officer, and measures to detect, respond to and recover from incidents — is July 2027. One obligation has applied since the effective date and is easy to miss: reportable cyber incidents must be reported to the National Response Center. Given the North Carolina Ports incident this month, US-regulated facilities should confirm their duty officers know the NRC reporting threshold and number without looking them up.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: USCG final rule summary — The Maritime Executive and ABS Group
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Rule effective 16 Jul 2025; training due 12 Jan 2026; full compliance July 2027
